subject: snail-eating snake
title: This Snake Has 25 Teeth on One Side and 15 on the Other. On Purpose

scenes.text: One snake has a lopsided jaw: far more teeth on the right than the left.
Iwasaki's snail-eater lives on a few small islands in southern Japan, and snails are its specialty.
Its lower jaw has about 25 teeth on the right side. And about 15 on the left.
Here's why. Most snail shells coil to the right, and the uneven jaw is built to reach into that spiral.
In experiments, it ate every right-coiled snail it was given. It managed only one in eight left-coiled ones.
So where this snake lives, left-coiled snails keep evolving. Its dinner is twisting away from it.

description:
Iwasaki's snail-eater has a lopsided jaw: about 25 teeth on the right side of its lower jaw and about 15 on the left.
The snake (Pareas iwasakii) lives only in the Yaeyama Islands at the southern end of Japan's Ryukyu chain and specialises in land snails. Most snails have shells that coil to the right (dextral), and the snake's asymmetric jaw is adapted to reach into that kind of opening. In feeding experiments by Masaki Hoso and colleagues (Biology Letters 2007; Nature Communications 2010) the snakes ate all the right-coiled snails they were offered but only 12.5 percent of the left-coiled ones. That gives rare left-coiled snails a survival advantage, and left-coiled lineages of Satsuma snails have evolved more often where the snake lives.
Which side would you bet on, the snake or the snail? Comment below.
first_comment: Left-coiled snails are rare almost everywhere on Earth, except where this snake hunts. Snake or snail: who wins in the end?
